deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a page of lecture notes (or excerpts) on ancient history, specifically the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt. It continues from f.168 (Ptolemy I Soter) and leads into f.170 (Ptolemy IV and V). Content in order:
(1) Ptolemy II Philadelphus, reigned 284–246. He was physically weak and could not lead the army himself. He is said to have had 33,000 cities. His half-brother Magas held Cyrene and tried to make himself independent, and a war followed. The notes date it 266–250 and say it ended well for Egypt. Philadelphus married Arsinoe (I), daughter of Lysimachus, repudiated her, and married his sister Arsinoe (II).
(2) Ptolemy III Euergetes reigned 25 years. He first waged war on Seleucus II Callinicus. A marginal note gives the reason: Laodice had had Berenice murdered. Euergetes won, and in 242 made a 10-year truce with Seleucus. He then campaigned east, reportedly subduing lands as far as the Indus, while his general took the west coast of Arabia. He died in 221.
(3) His son Ptolemy IV Philopator succeeded him.
There are no derivations, formulas or computations. The only numbers are regnal and war dates. The internal arithmetic is consistent: 246 − 25 = 221 matches 'regierte 25 Jahr' and †221. The hand and the subject (a course of the Heeren/Spittler type on ancient states) suggest student notes, possibly not by Gauss himself. This cannot be decided from the image alone.
errors: Historical: the '33000 Städte' echoes Theocritus, Idyll 17, which gives 33,333 cities. It is a panegyric figure, not a fact.

Historical: the war dated 266–250 does not correspond to a single known conflict. Magas' secession and his attack on Egypt fall c. 275/274 (First Syrian War context). The Chremonidean War was c. 267–261 and the Second Syrian War c. 260–253. The note conflates these.
Historical: the Third Syrian (Laodicean) War ended c. 241. The '10-year truce' is from Justin, and modern dating would put it in 241 rather than 242.
Historical: Ptolemy III's eastern conquests 'bis an den Indus' exaggerate the Adulis inscription's claims (Mesopotamia, Persis, Bactria). The extent is doubtful.
Historical: Ptolemy III's death is now usually dated to late 222 BC. 221 is the conventional older date.

results.what: Outline of Ptolemaic history (Ptolemy II–IV): reigns, marriages, Syrian wars
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th/19th-century university history lectures (e.g., A. H. L. Heeren, Göttingen), based on Justin, Polybius, Theocritus

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical history notes on the Ptolemies, probably lecture notes, with no mathematical content at all.

checkable.asserts: Length of Philadelphus' reign per the notes' dates (38 years)
Euergetes reigning 25 years from 246 is consistent with his death in 221 as stated
Duration of the war against Magas/Syria as dated in the notes
Length of Philopator's reign per the next page

transcription_corrections: Line 4: 'Magas dem er Cyrene entriss[?]' is uncertain in the image. The sense is more likely 'Magas, der Cyrene [inne hatte/entriss] und sich unabhängig machen wollte', since Magas, not Philadelphus, held Cyrene.
Line 11: 'Anfangs führte er einen Krieg' is correct reading (the image shows 'Anfangs führte').
Line 11: the image spells 'Sekucus' (i.e., Seleucus) and 'Callinicus'. The transcription normalizes this correctly.
The marginal addition 'weil Laodice d. Berenice hatte morden lassen' sits in the right margin beside 'Evergetes'. It explains the cause of the war and is correctly placed.
'Nun ging er nach Indien[?]': the reading is plausible from the image, consistent with 'bis an den Indus'.
'†221' at the end of the Arabia sentence refers to Euergetes' death, not to the general.
